title: The Glorious Zion
overview: Psalm 87 is a poetic celebration of Zion, the city of God, emphasizing its divine foundation and unique status among the nations. The psalm highlights God's special love for Zion, portraying it as the birthplace of many peoples, including foreign nations, who are spiritually identified with it. This chapter underscores the theme of God's sovereign choice and the inclusion of Gentiles within His covenant community. It reflects the joy and honor of being counted among God's people and anticipates the universal recognition of Zion’s spiritual significance. Positioned within the Psalter, Psalm 87 serves as a hymn of praise that elevates Zion as the center of God's redemptive plan and the gathering place of all who belong to Him.
structure:
**Verses 1-3: The Foundation and Divine Love for Zion.** The psalm opens by declaring Zion’s divine foundation in the holy mountains and God’s special love for its gates, setting Zion apart above all dwellings of Jacob. The city is praised for its glorious reputation.

**Verses 4-6: The Inclusion of Nations and Divine Registration.** The psalmist mentions foreign nations—Rahab (Egypt), Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia—signifying the inclusion of Gentiles who are spiritually born in Zion. God Himself records those born there, affirming their belonging.

**Verse 7: The Joyful Worship in Zion.** The chapter concludes with a vision of worship, where singers and instrumentalists gather in Zion, symbolizing the abundant spiritual life and blessings flowing from the city as the source of all springs.

keyVerses.text: The LORD loveth the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights God's special affection for Zion, emphasizing its unique status as the chosen place of His presence and blessing. It sets the tone for the psalm's theme of divine favor and election.

keyVerses.text: I will make mention of Rahab and Babylon to them that know me: behold Philistia, and Tyre, with Ethiopia; this man was born there.
keyVerses.significance: This verse signifies the inclusion of Gentile nations into the spiritual family of Zion, indicating God's sovereign grace extends beyond Israel. It foreshadows the universal scope of God's redemptive plan.

keyVerses.text: The LORD shall count, when he writeth up the people, that this man was born there. Selah.
keyVerses.significance: This verse underscores God's active role in recording and acknowledging those who belong to Zion, affirming divine election and the certainty of belonging to God's covenant community.

keyVerses.text: As well the singers as the players on instruments shall be there: all my springs are in thee.
keyVerses.significance: The closing verse portrays Zion as the source of spiritual vitality and worship, symbolizing the joy and life that flow from being united with God in His holy city.

characters.name: The LORD
characters.description: God is the central figure who establishes Zion, loves its gates, and records the people born there. His sovereign choice and blessing define the city's significance.

characters.name: Zion
characters.description: Personified as the city of God, Zion is the spiritual foundation and birthplace of God's people, including Gentiles. It represents God's chosen dwelling and the center of worship.

characters.name: Nations (Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, Ethiopia)
characters.description: These represent foreign peoples who are spiritually identified with Zion, illustrating the inclusion of Gentiles in God's covenant community.

themes.description: The psalm emphasizes God's sovereign choice of Zion as His special dwelling and the inclusion of its inhabitants in His covenant, reflecting the biblical theme of election.
By naming foreign nations as born in Zion, the psalm reveals God's plan to incorporate Gentiles into His people, anticipating the New Testament revelation of the church.
The presence of singers and musicians symbolizes the joy and spiritual vitality that characterize life in Zion, emphasizing worship as central to the believer’s identity.
God’s act of writing up the people born in Zion highlights His faithfulness in preserving His covenant community and ensuring their eternal belonging.

historicalContext: Psalm 87 is attributed to the sons of Korah, a Levitical family responsible for temple worship, likely composed during or after the post-exilic period when Jerusalem’s restoration was a central concern. The holy mountains refer to the elevated site of Zion, Jerusalem, in the land of Judah, which was the political and religious center of Israel. The mention of foreign nations such as Rahab (Egypt), Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia reflects the geopolitical realities of the ancient Near East, where these peoples were known neighbors or conquerors of Israel. The psalm reflects the hope and theological affirmation that despite political turmoil, Zion remains the divinely chosen city, and its spiritual influence extends beyond ethnic Israel.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology sees Psalm 87 as affirming God’s sovereign election of His people and the inclusion of the Gentiles into the covenant community through Christ. The psalm anticipates the spiritual birth and regeneration that unite believers to Zion, the city of God.

Dispensational interpreters emphasize the literal future fulfillment of Zion’s exaltation and the gathering of nations to Jerusalem in the millennial kingdom. The psalm is viewed as prophetic of the physical restoration of Israel and the inclusion of Gentiles in that era.

Early church interpreters often allegorized Zion as the Church, the spiritual Jerusalem, where believers from all nations are born anew. They saw the psalm as celebrating the unity of Jews and Gentiles in Christ.

crossReferences.connection: Like Psalm 87, Isaiah speaks of many nations coming to the mountain of the Lord, emphasizing Zion’s role as a spiritual center for all peoples.
Jesus’ teaching on being 'born again' connects with the psalm’s theme of spiritual birth in Zion, highlighting new life in God’s kingdom.
Paul’s metaphor of Gentiles being grafted into the olive tree parallels Psalm 87’s inclusion of foreign nations as born in Zion.
The heavenly Jerusalem is described as the city of the living God, echoing Zion’s exalted status in Psalm 87.
The New Jerusalem coming down from heaven fulfills the vision of Zion as the eternal dwelling place of God’s people.

application: Trust in God’s sovereign choice and love for His people, knowing He has established a firm foundation for believers.
Embrace the spiritual unity of all believers, regardless of background, as part of God’s covenant community.
Cultivate a heart of worship and joy, recognizing that spiritual vitality flows from being connected to God’s presence.
Rejoice that God actively records and remembers those who belong to Him, providing assurance of salvation.
Pray for the peace and prosperity of Zion, the city of God, as a model for seeking God’s kingdom on earth.
Share the gospel confidently, knowing that God includes all nations in His redemptive plan.
conclusion: Psalm 87 stands as a timeless hymn celebrating Zion’s divine foundation, God’s special love, and the inclusion of all peoples into His spiritual family. It affirms the joy and worship that flow from belonging to God’s city and the assurance that God Himself records His people. For believers today, it is a reminder of the unity found in Christ, the privilege of being part of God’s covenant community, and the call to worship with gladness. This psalm encourages faithfulness, hope, and active participation in the spiritual life centered on God’s eternal city.
timeline: c. 10th–6th century BC, likely post-exilic period (after 538 BC) reflecting restoration themes

outline.heading: The Divine Foundation of Zion
outline.description: The psalm opens by establishing Zion’s sacred foundation and God’s special love for its gates, highlighting its exalted status among the dwellings of Jacob.

outline.heading: The Inclusion of Foreign Nations
outline.description: God mentions various Gentile nations as being born in Zion, signifying the spiritual inclusion of all peoples into God’s covenant community and His sovereign record-keeping.

outline.heading: Joyful Worship in Zion
outline.description: The psalm concludes with a vision of worship where singers and musicians gather, symbolizing the abundant spiritual life and blessings flowing from Zion.
